query: What are the published power numbers, mixing times and energy dissipation rates for magnetic stir bars (cylindrical, oval, octagonal, egg-shaped) in round-bottom flasks or beakers, as a function of Reynolds number, stir rate and flask size? Give correlations or numbers with units (Np versus Re, mixing time theta95 versus rpm, epsilon in W/kg), the bar and vessel geometry and solvent used, and cite the primary sources (for example work from the Noel group on stirring in organic synthesis, Bourne, Nienow, Mahmoudi/Hartman or other studies of magnetic stirrer hydrodynamics), with DOI where available.

## Magnetic stir-bar hydrodynamics: what the primary sources establish

**The requested numerical catalogue cannot be verified from the available primary texts.** They provide several magnetic-bar geometries and mixing observations, but no measured bar-specific power-number correlation, \(N_P\) versus \(Re\), or bulk energy-dissipation rate in W kg⁻¹ for cylindrical, oval, octagonal, or egg-shaped bars in ordinary beakers or round-bottom flasks. Nor do their reported mixing endpoints establish a comparable \(\theta_{95}\)-versus-rpm series. Reporting coefficients or W kg⁻¹ values for those configurations would therefore imply measurements that the inspected sources do not provide. (bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 2-4, bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 2-4, gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 7-11)

The following comparison separates **measured mixing endpoints** from operating conditions and hydrodynamic measurements. The JetMixer is included as a bar-like bottom-contacting mixer, **not** as an ordinary laboratory stir bar. (bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 2-4, bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 2-4, gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 15-19)

| Primary source and configuration | Vessel and liquid | Magnetic element | Stir rate and Reynolds number | Published mixing result | Published power data |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bilgen et al. (2005), cylindrical spinner flask SF1 | 120 mL; vessel diameter T = 6.3 cm; aqueous HCl, NaOH, and phenolphthalein | Bar length L = 3.81 cm; L/T = 0.61 | 30, 50, and 80 rpm; Re = N L²/ν | Mixing time was plotted against rpm and Re, but exact values were not tabulated. Endpoint was disappearance of pink phenolphthalein, not θ95. | Power, Np, and ε: **not reported** (bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 2-4, bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 5-6) |
| Bilgen et al. (2005), wavy-wall vessels W1 and W1a | 120 mL; average vessel diameter T = 6.7 cm; aqueous HCl, NaOH, and phenolphthalein; wave amplitudes 0.45 and 0.65 cm | Bar length L = 3.81 cm; L/T = 0.57 | 30, 50, and 80 rpm; Re = N L²/ν | Mixing time was plotted but exact values were not tabulated. Endpoint was phenolphthalein disappearance, not θ95. The larger wave amplitude shortened mixing relative to SF1 at 50 rpm. | Power, Np, and ε: **not reported** (bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 2-4, bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 5-6) |
| Bilgen et al. (2006), prototype wavy-wall bioreactor | 120 mL glass vessel; cell-culture medium; ν = 0.971 cSt; density = 1.03 g/cm³ | Octagonal bar, 3.81 cm long and 0.79 cm outer diameter | 50.0 rpm; Re = N L²/ν = 1246 | PIV hydrodynamics and local shear and Reynolds stresses were measured; θ95 was not reported. | Power, Np, and mean ε: **not reported** (bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 2-4) |
| Bilgen et al. (2006), dynamically similar PIV model | 330 mL acrylic vessel; 57 wt% zinc iodide and 0.5 wt% sodium bisulfite solution; ν = 1.68 cSt; density = 1.90 g/cm³ | Scaled octagonal bar, 5.33 cm long and 1.10 cm outer diameter | 44.2 rpm; Re = 1246 ± 14 | PIV velocity and stress fields were measured; θ95 was not reported. | Power, Np, and mean ε: **not reported** (bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 2-4) |
| Gikanga et al. (2017), small-scale SB1–SB4 tests | 200 mL protein or monoclonal-antibody formulation in a flat-base 500 mL glass beaker or Erlenmeyer flask | SB1: cylindrical PTFE-coated bar, 50.96 × 9.66 mm; SB2: SB1 with a central plastic ring, maximum diameter 10.43 mm; SB3: 38.11 × 7.97 mm bar in a tri-stand; SB4: SB1 in a top-entry arrangement | 180 rpm for 1–2 h; Re not reported | Protein-particle formation rather than bulk mixing time was measured; θ95 was not reported. | Power, Np, and ε: **not reported** (gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 7-11, gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 15-19) |
| Gikanga et al. (2017), JetMixer | 45 L in a 50 L disposable container; 55 wt% sucrose solution; viscosity 25 cP; green-dye tracer | Bottom-contacting, magnetically impelled bar-like turbine; effective diameter or length 7.2 cm | 230 rpm; tip speed 0.84 m/s; Re not reported | Mixing time was 10 min to constant UV absorbance and visual homogeneity. This dye-plateau endpoint was not explicitly θ95. | Power, Np, and ε: **not reported** (gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 15-19, gikanga2017processingimpacton media 683ebccb) |


*Table: Primary-text-verified geometries, operating conditions, and mixing endpoints for magnetic bars and a bar-like JetMixer. “Not reported” applies only to these cited experiments, not necessarily to the broader literature.*

### Mixing times, geometry, and Reynolds number

Bilgen, Chang-Mateu and Barabino, *Biotechnology and Bioengineering* **92** (2005), 907–919, DOI [10.1002/bit.20667](https://doi.org/10.1002/bit.20667), measured mixing in 120-mL conventional spinner flasks and wavy-walled variants using a 3.81-cm magnetic bar. Their Figure 3 plots time in seconds at **30, 50, and 80 rpm**, but the endpoint is disappearance of pink phenolphthalein after an aqueous acid addition—not a defined 95% concentration approach. The accessible text does not tabulate the plotted times, and the figure could not be inspected reliably here; exact seconds should not be inferred. At **50 rpm**, increasing wall-wave amplitude from **0.45 to 0.65 cm** reduced the reported mixing time to approximately **35% below** that of the conventional flask. The same paper’s **23.6 ± 0.2 min** and **27.0 ± 2.5 min** values are *continuous-flow mean residence times* at 50 rpm, not batch mixing times. These vessels are spinner-flask geometries, not round-bottom synthetic flasks. (bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 2-4, bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 4-5, bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 5-6, bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 6-8)

Bilgen and colleagues, *Biotechnology and Bioengineering* **95** (2006), 1009–1022, DOI [10.1002/bit.20775](https://doi.org/10.1002/bit.20775), explicitly identify an **octagonal-cross-section** magnetic bar. Their 120-mL glass, wavy-wall prototype used a **3.81-cm-long × 0.79-cm-outer-diameter** bar at **50 rpm** in cell-culture medium (kinematic viscosity **0.971 cSt**), giving their stated \(Re=1246\). A dynamically similar 330-mL acrylic PIV model used a **5.33 × 1.10 cm** bar at **44.2 rpm** in a zinc-iodide/sodium-bisulfite solution (**1.68 cSt**) at the same Reynolds number. The study reports velocity and local stress fields, **not** \(\theta_{95}\), shaft/bar power, or volume-averaged \(\varepsilon\). Its turbulent kinetic energy and stresses must not be relabelled as W kg⁻¹ dissipation. (bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 2-4, bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 4-5, bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 6-9, bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 9-11)

Gikanga and co-workers, *PDA Journal of Pharmaceutical Science and Technology* **71** (2017), 172–188, DOI [10.5731/pdajpst.2016.006726](https://doi.org/10.5731/pdajpst.2016.006726), tested PTFE-coated bars in **200 mL** of protein formulation in flat-bottom **500-mL beakers or Erlenmeyer flasks** at **180 rpm**. Their standard bar was **50.96 × 9.66 mm**; other arrangements included that bar with a central ring and a **38.11 × 7.97 mm** bar held in a stand. Those tests concern protein-particle formation; they do **not** supply a macromixing time or bar power measurement. In a separate **45-L**, bar-like JetMixer experiment, **55 wt% sucrose solution** of **25 cP** reached constant dye absorbance and visual homogeneity in **10 min** at the Table IV low-speed setting of **230 rpm** (effective element diameter **7.2 cm**). This is a dye-plateau criterion, **not explicitly \(\theta_{95}\)**, and cannot be transferred to a beaker or round-bottom flask. (gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 7-11, gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 15-19, gikanga2017processingimpacton media 683ebccb)

For the Bilgen studies, the explicitly defined bar Reynolds number is \(Re=NL^2/\nu=\rho NL^2/\mu\), where \(N\) is the **actual bar rotations per second** and \(L\) is bar *length*, rather than its cross-sectional diameter. For example, applying that definition to the 2005 study’s 3.81-cm bar at 30, 50, and 80 rpm gives approximately **725, 1,208, and 1,933**, respectively, **if** \(\nu=1.00\) cSt. These three values are calculations for an assumed water-like viscosity, **not published Reynolds values for its acid–base solutions**; they should not replace the 2006 paper’s stated \(Re=1246\), which uses its measured medium viscosity. (bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 2-4, bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 5-6, bilgen2006flowcharacterizationof pages 2-4)

### Power number and dissipation: a consequential exclusion

The relevant definitions are \(N_P=P/(\rho N^3L^5)\) and mean specific dissipation \(\bar\varepsilon=P/(\rho V)=N_PN^3L^5/V\), in **W kg⁻¹**. They permit conversion *only after liquid-delivered bar power* \(P\)—or a power number measured for that bar, fluid, and vessel—is known. Stirrer-plate electrical consumption alone is not such a measurement. None of the accessible bar experiments above provides the necessary power. In particular, the **\(N_P=0.3\)** and **\(0.65\)** listed by Gikanga *belong to separate Lightnin axial-flow and bottom-mounted impellers*, respectively; assigning either number to their small PTFE bars or the JetMixer would be erroneous. (gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 7-11, gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 11-15)

A second tempting set of W kg⁻¹ numbers is likewise **not magnetic-bar evidence**: Fyfe and colleagues’ 2024 DOI [10.1021/acs.oprd.4c00229](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.oprd.4c00229) gives *Dynochem-calculated* power per mass of **0.001, 0.003, and 0.019 W kg⁻¹** without baffles at 120, 200, and 400 rpm, and **0.001, 0.006, and 0.048 W kg⁻¹** with baffles. Its vessel is a **2-L overhead-stirred tank with a four-bladed pitched-blade turbine**. These are not measurements or predictions for a magnetic bar. Likewise, its tabulated blend times must not be presented as bar \(\theta_{95}\) values. (fyfe2024acomputervision pages 1-3, fyfe2024acomputervision pages 4-5, fyfe2024acomputervision pages 3-4)

**Scope of the remaining gap.** Mahmud and colleagues’ magnetic-stirrer free-surface study, *Chemical Engineering Science* **64** (2009), 4197–4209, DOI [10.1016/j.ces.2009.06.059](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2009.06.059), is identifiable, but its primary text was unavailable here, so no \(N_P\), \(\theta_{95}\), or \(\varepsilon\) values can responsibly be extracted from it. Allonneau and colleagues’ magnetic-bar reactor study, *Biochemical Engineering Journal* **96** (2015), 29–37, DOI [10.1016/j.bej.2014.12.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bej.2014.12.005), was likewise not available for numerical verification. The retrieved evidence does **not** establish shape-resolved correlations for **oval or egg-shaped** bars, solvent-specific results for ordinary organic-synthesis round-bottom flasks, or such a data set attributable to Noël, Bourne, Nienow, or Mahmoudi/Hartman. Absence of verification here is **not** a claim that no such work exists; it is the boundary of the substantiated answer. (salho2024studytheeffect pages 39-42, bilgen2005characterizationofmixing pages 2-4, gikanga2017processingimpacton pages 15-19)
